1:
Clarke treats the opening clause as a key to passages elsewhere. The Hebrew verb for justify is used here exactly as the corresponding Greek verb is sometimes used by Paul, not to make just but to acquit, to declare innocent, to remit punishment or give reasons why a man should not be punished; so the magistrates are to acquit the righteous, and the Greek version uses the very word Paul uses of a sinner's justification. Wesley glosses it the same way in a line, acquitting from guilt and false accusation and freeing from punishment. Henry sets out the procedure the verse presupposes: accuser and accused brought face to face before the judges, acquittal where the proof falls short, and where the charge is made out the conviction of the accused counts as a justification of the accuser as righteous in the prosecution. He adds the reciprocal principle from Proverbs, that justifying the wicked is as much an abomination as condemning the righteous. Gill and Wesley both explain why scourging comes next, that a great many precepts carry no stated penalty, and that by constant Jewish practice the breach of these was punished with stripes.

Two things about the beating are stressed by everyone: that it happen in the judge's presence, and that the count be kept. Keil and Delitzsch supply the physical detail, that the strokes were administered with a stick upon the back, and identify the posture from Egyptian monuments where the culprit lies flat on the ground, held fast by hands and feet, and is beaten before the judge. Clarke reports the same procedure surviving in China, where the culprit receives the punishment in the magistrate's presence so that the officers can transgress the law neither by indulgence nor by severity. Calvin reads the whole provision as a restraint on zeal rather than a schedule of penalties, noting that no equal measure is prescribed and that judges otherwise not unjust are often as severe on small offences as on crimes; the requirement that they be present is there so that their authority may prevent excess. He draws the argument outward, that since God spares the guilty so far as to repress even just severity, much more will he have regard to innocent blood, and much less will he tolerate private violence between brothers.

On the reduction to thirty-nine, Gill gives the reasoning and the mechanics. The rabbinic rule reads the number as the one next to forty, joining the last word of one verse to the first of the next; and since the scourge was made with three lashes, each stroke counted as three stripes, so that thirteen strokes made thirty-nine and a fourteenth would have overshot by two. He notes the apostle suffered the full extremity of it as then understood. Wesley calls the practice not superstition but prudent caution, lest through mistake or forgetfulness they pass a bound they were commanded to keep. On the reason given for the limit the readings differ slightly. Keil and Delitzsch make it partly medical and partly social, since more strokes would endanger health and life and also disgrace the man, adding that one who deserved worse was to be executed instead; Wesley offers the same two senses as alternatives, contempt from the usage itself or from the deformity excessive beating might produce. Clarke uses the verse for a long protest against sentences of three hundred or a thousand lashes, and recounts a flogging that helped wreck an embassy to China.
4:
The precept assumes a threshing method the commentators take trouble to describe. Keil and Delitzsch have oxen yoked together and driven to and fro over corn strewn on the floor so that the grains are kicked out by their hoofs, and report that both the method and the custom of leaving the animals unmuzzled survive in the East, adding drily that the Mosaic injunctions are not so strictly observed there by the Christians as by the Mohammedans. Clarke, drawing on a traveller's account of Barbary, adds that mules and horses were often used instead of oxen, three or four tied by the neck and whipped round the floor; that the work was done in the open air on a level plot daubed over with cow dung to keep down the dust, so that a good deal of earth and gravel was taken up with the grain and the straw shattered to pieces — a circumstance he finds alluded to where a king is said to have made Israel like the dust by threshing. From Bengal he reports that some muzzle the ox and some do not, according to the farmer's disposition.

Gill collects what else the prohibition covers, since a muzzle is only one way of keeping a working animal from the grain. From Maimonides he lists four devices the law forbids: putting a thorn in the creature's mouth, causing a lion to lie down beside it, causing its calf to lie down outside the floor, and spreading a skin over the top of the corn. From Aelian he adds a method used in some countries, of besmearing the ox's nostrils with cow dung, which the animal found so disagreeable that it would not feed. The point of the list is that the commandment is aimed at the intention rather than the instrument.

On the application all of them follow the apostle, and Calvin says why that is legitimate. Paul is the faithful expositor of the passage, declaring that God had no other design in delivering it than that the labourer should not be defrauded of his hire, and himself meeting the objection that oxen and men are different by saying that God does not care for oxen but spoke for the sake of those who labour. Calvin will not let the literal sense drop out even so: men are instructed in equity to the point of being bound to exercise it toward brute animals, and if we owe subsistence to beasts we must not wait to be pressed before paying men their due. Keil and Delitzsch call the sentence proverbial rather than merely literal; Clarke reports Le Clerc taking it as wholly symbolical, and himself reads it as teaching kindness to servants and labourers and especially to those who minister in holy things. Henry and Wesley reach the same place independently, Henry that we must be not only just but kind to those employed for the good of our better part, Wesley that humanity to beasts implies much more toward the men who labour for us.
5:
Who counts as a brother dwelling together is the first question, and Calvin answers it against the plain word. The term does not mean actual brothers but cousins and other kinsmen whose marriage with the widow would not have been incestuous, since otherwise God would contradict himself, having forbidden a man to uncover his brother's nakedness; and he takes Boaz for proof, who married Ruth not as the brother of her deceased husband but only as his near kinsman. Gill and Wesley keep the narrower sense while stretching the dwelling. Gill takes it of living in the same house, brothers brought up together in their father's house, but reports the Targum and Jarchi referring it instead to being united in one inheritance, so that the place of residence does not matter; he adds from Maimonides that only brothers on the father's side are meant, since there is no brotherhood but on the father's side. Wesley makes the residence practical, that if the next brother had moved to remote parts or been carried into captivity the widow was free to marry the next kinsman living where she was.

On what the law is for, three purposes are named and they do not compete. Keil and Delitzsch give the mechanism, that the first-born was to stand upon the name of the deceased, placed in his family and recognised as heir of his property so that the dead man's name should not be blotted out. Calvin makes it a property provision above all, since the object is that no one be obliged to leave what he has to strangers, and God so far provides even for the dying that what they could not resign without regret is preserved to their offspring; on his reading a kinsman who fails to obviate the childlessness commits a kind of theft. Wesley adds a purpose peculiar to the nation, that the distinction of tribes and families be kept up so that the Messiah might be discovered by the family from which he was to come. Henry supplies the human reason underneath, that under that dispensation men had no such clear prospect of living beyond death as the gospel has since given, and were therefore the more desirous to live in their posterity, an innocent desire which this law in some measure gratified.

Clarke admits it is difficult to find the reason of the ceremonies of degradation, and offers what he can. The shoe was perhaps an emblem of power, so that stripping it off represented deprivation of authority; Wesley says the same and adds the second edge, that going barefoot was the condition of the meanest servants, so the loosing marked the man unworthy to be among freemen. On the spitting Clarke corrects the English, reporting that the Jews, whom he calls the legitimate judges in the case, hold it was not into the face but before the face on the ground, which is how travellers say detestation is still expressed in the East; and he adds a grammatical note on the preposition, which can mean before as well as in. Gill supplies the procedure around it, that the time and place were appointed the evening before by three rabbins and two witnesses, and the woman was ordered to come fasting. On the name that follows, Gill observes that not the man's personal name but his family was so called, the mark of infamy passing to his house; Wesley makes the same point and calls it a lasting blot.
11:
Gill sets the scene plainly, that the men have quarrelled and come to blows and are striving for mastery, each to be the one who beats the other. Calvin concedes at once that the law is apparently harsh, and then argues that its very severity is the point: it shows how pleasing modesty is to God and how thoroughly he abominates indecency. He calls the act inexcusable effrontery, a wilful assault on the part of the body from whose sight and touch chaste women naturally recoil.

From that severity Calvin draws an inference by proportion. If the thing was punished so heavily when done in the heat of a quarrel, where the agitation of the mind is at least some excuse for excess, then lasciviousness done deliberately out of lust would be pardoned still less; and he holds that judges were bound to reason in the same way, arguing from the less to the greater whenever they punished obscenity. The added warning that the eye shall not pity is there, on his reading, precisely so that the harshness of the sentence should not make those charged with it tender and remiss in carrying it out. Gill assigns the execution carefully: the hand was to be cut off not by the man she had seized nor by any bystander but by the civil magistrate or at his order, and the severity was aimed at deterring women who on such occasions are passionate and inconsiderate.

Whether the sentence was ever carried out literally Gill leaves open. He reports that the Jewish writers interpret the words not of an actual amputation but of a valuable consideration, a price set upon the hand, naming Jarchi for that reading; and that Aben Ezra compares the case with the law of retaliation, eye for eye, which the same writers commonly understand of paying a price for what was lost rather than of exacting the member itself. On that construction the hand is forfeit only if she does not redeem it.

The weights that follow are literally a stone and a stone, and Clarke explains why. Weights were anciently made of stone, and a dishonest trader kept two sets, a heavy one to buy his neighbour's wares by and a light one to sell his own; he adds that the practice was once common in Britain, where smooth round stones were chosen by country people for selling goods by the pound, and that the term a stone weight survives although lead or iron is now the counterpoise. Gill notes the measure named in the next verse is likewise doubled in the Hebrew, an ephah and an ephah. Henry catches the force of the prohibition, that they were not merely forbidden to use false weights but to have them, not in the bag and not in the house, since possessing them is a standing temptation; and he observes that the two together cheat at both ends, as with the prophet's ephah made small for selling corn and shekel made great for weighing the money received. He adds the reason the passage itself gives, that what is the rule of justice must itself be just, or it becomes a constant cheat, and notes that the promise attached is length of days while the sanction is that not only unrighteousness but all who do unrighteously are an abomination.
17:
The aggravations of the offence are counted up rather than the offence itself. Calvin makes the attack unjust in the first place, since Israel was inflicting neither injury nor loss and was merely passing peaceably toward another land; but he presses a second charge harder, that the Amalekites did not spare their own kindred and so cast away the feelings of nature, being descendants of Esau and therefore sprung with Israel from the one ancestor. Wesley aggravates it differently, that this was done to a people long exercised with sore afflictions, to whom pity was owed by the laws of nature and humanity, and for whose rescue God had appeared so gloriously that the Amalekites could not have been ignorant of it. Gill fixes the manner: they met Israel by the way not with provisions, which would have been kindness to travellers, but sword in hand, to stop the journey and make captives. Keil and Delitzsch locate the point of attack at the rear, among all the enfeebled who lagged behind when the people were faint and weary.

The clause that they feared not God is where Calvin concentrates. He refuses to take it in its ordinary sense, holding that it expresses a deliberate rebellion rather than mere irreligion, since the promise given to Abraham and Isaac could not have been unknown to a people descended from Esau. He also meets the objection that the command sits ill with religion, since it appears to order retaliation for an injury received. His answer is that the people are not stimulated to vindictive feeling but commanded to punish the sins of Amalek with the same severity as those of the other nations, and that although private motives seem to be appealed to when the cruelty is recounted, the intention of the Legislator must be judged by his nature, no angry or hateful passion being capable of God's approval; the command was therefore such as could be obeyed with well-regulated zeal. Keil and Delitzsch set the passage in its place at the close of the discourse, as the warning that love toward neighbour, stranger and foe alike was not to degenerate into weakness or indifference toward open ungodliness.

On the timing of the order Gill is exact, observing that rest from all enemies round about means more than the conquest of Canaan: it means freedom from the neighbouring nations as well, Moabites, Midianites, Edomites, Ammonites and Philistines, so that the command took effect neither immediately after the conquest nor during the period of the judges, when Israel was harassed continually, but only in the reign of the first king. Clarke carries the reckoning to its end, supposing the final accomplishment to be the death of Haman and his ten sons, from which time the name of Amalek was blotted out from under heaven; and he adds that through every period of their history it might truly be said of them that they feared not God. Henry turns the whole to warning and to allegory at once, that every persecutor of God's people should take the case for a warning, since the longer judgment is delayed the more dreadful it is at last, and that Amalek may remind us of the enemies of our own souls.
